values.value: • Use the healthy deal size to protect value and avoid unnecessary discounting. • Tie commercials to business impact, scale, implementation value, and future upside. • Confirm that the scope and pricing remain aligned with the buyer's desired outcome. • Make sure a bigger deal still feels easy to approve through good structuring. • Protect margin by selling value before concession.

Yes

• Check whether the smaller deal size is a tactical entry point or a sign of scope weakness. • Explore upsell elements, phased expansion, or add-ons that genuinely improve buyer outcomes. • Do not push for more size unless the value case supports it. • Protect winability while looking for smart expansion. • A slightly smaller deal can still be the right first step.
17|Less by 10%
Buyer may say, 'Can we start smaller?' Response: 'Yes, if that still solves the right problem. Let us make sure the smaller scope remains meaningful and expandable.'
Tighten scope or add value proof before negotiating down. Small gaps can often be bridged without price cuts.
Risk: Early price pressure risk.
Ask: 'Is the concern about total price, phase-one size, or confidence in outcome?'
Less by 10%

• Challenge whether the deal has been over-narrowed or heavily price-pressured. • Ask what has been removed and whether the current scope still solves the real problem. • Explore a stronger phased roadmap so phase one is smaller but future value is visible. • Avoid accepting a poor commercial shape without understanding why it shrank. • Reset the deal around value, not only around what is easiest to approve.
17|Much less
Buyer may say, 'This is all we can consider right now.' Response: 'Understood. Then let us structure phase one carefully so it delivers value and keeps room for the right expansion later.'
Do not chase the full scope at the wrong price. Repackage the offer into a smaller, high-value starting point.
High risk: Value and price are misaligned.
Say: 'Rather than force a misfit commercial, let us shape a first phase that is easier to approve.'
Much less

• Benchmark the current commercial shape against similar customer size, use case, and line of business. • Check if you have under-scoped, under-priced, or misunderstood the buyer's true requirement. • Use internal deal references to sanity-check the opportunity value. • Then decide whether to expand scope, hold position, or keep it as an entry deal. • You need a clear value benchmark before finalising commercials.
17|Don't know
Buyer may say, 'We have not thought about ideal deal size.' Response: 'That is fine. I will benchmark this against similar situations so we can judge whether the scope is right.'
Benchmark this deal against similar accounts before you negotiate. Confidence comes from context, not instinct.
Risk: Weak price strategy.
Ask: 'How does this compare with what similar customers have approved for a similar scope?'
Don't know
Is the deal size equal to or greater than the target average deal size of similar customer size and Line of business?
